title: Lead Quality Score for Business Finance Leads | Loanleaf
description: How the Loanleaf lead quality score from 0 to 100 works, how fundability sets the price, and how to use both when choosing business finance leads.
summary: Every Loanleaf lead carries a quality score from 0 to 100, built from credit history, time trading, revenue, urgency and existing debt. Separately, a lead's price in credits reflects its fundability. Used together, the two help you pick leads that fit your lenders and your budget.

blocks: The quality score is a single number from 0 to 100 shown on every lead in the Opportunities list. It summarises how strong the enquiry looks from the answers the business owner gave on the form.

It is a guide, not a promise. A high score tells you the answers look favourable. It does not tell you whether a particular lender will say yes, because lenders weigh things the form does not ask about.
You see the score before you buy, alongside the amount, purpose, timeline, revenue, trading time, credit history and existing finance. It is one input among several, which is how it works best.
The score is based on five answers from the enquiry form:

list: Credit history: whether the business has had missed payments, defaults or CCJs in the last 6 years (No, Yes or Not sure).
Time trading: 6 to 12 months, 1 to 2 years, 2 to 5 years or 5+ years.
Urgency: as soon as possible, within 2 weeks, within a month, or just exploring options.
Existing debt: whether the business already has finance, and how much is left to repay and what the monthly repayments are.

blocks: All of these are things the business told us. Nothing is scraped or bought in. The score does not include anything the form does not ask, such as sector, property value or bank statement data.

The price of a lead is a separate calculation from the score, though they often move together. Price reflects fundability: how likely the enquiry is to turn into a funded deal. It uses loan size, revenue, time trading, credit history and affordability.

Affordability is the factor that most separates price from score. It asks whether the amount requested is realistic for the business's revenue. A £25,000 request from a business with £100k to £250k revenue is realistic. A £5m request from the same business is not.

That is why a lead can have a decent score but a very low price. The business may look fine on credit and trading time, but if it is asking for far more than its revenue could support, the model prices it at or near the 20 credit minimum. The full price range is covered on the pricing page.
Look at both numbers, then at the lead itself. Here is how the combinations tend to read.

list: High score, higher price: an established business with a sensible ask. Expect to pay more, and expect a better chance of completing.
High score, low price: check the amount against the revenue. The ask may be unrealistic, so a smaller facility could be the real opportunity.
Lower score, lower price: may suit brokers who work adverse credit, newer businesses or specialist lenders, where the cost per lead matters.

blocks: The point is that a low price is not a warning and a high price is not a guarantee. They tell you different things.

sections.h2: Using the score to choose leads
blocks: Start with what you can actually place. If your lenders do not touch adverse credit, filter to clean credit first, then use the score to rank what is left. If you specialise in younger businesses, do not rule out lower scores that come from trading time alone.

Match the lead to your cost of acquisition. If you budget a set number of credits per funded deal, a cheaper lead with a middling score may give you more attempts for the same spend than one expensive lead.

Check urgency. A lead marked as needing funds as soon as possible is a call to make first, whatever its score. Someone "just exploring options" may be worth a follow-up sequence rather than an immediate hard sell. Our guide to speed to lead covers how to prioritise.

Auto-buy criteria include loan size range, revenue bands, purposes, time trading and clean credit only, plus limits on leads per day, credits per day, credits per month and the maximum credits per lead.

The practical way to use the score is through those criteria. Clean credit only and a minimum time trading shape the score of what you receive. The maximum credits per lead caps how much you pay for the most fundable enquiries.

If a lead is above your per-lead maximum, it is left for you to buy manually and you get an email alert, so a strong lead is not lost just because it sits above your cap. See auto-buy for the full settings.

sections.h2: What the score cannot tell you
blocks: Be clear about the limits. The form does not ask for card takings or card machine turnover, property value or loan to value, the address of a property, whether it is residential or commercial investment, planning status, sector, director names or bank statements.

Those are exactly the things many lenders care about. A high score on a commercial property enquiry does not tell you whether the security stacks up. You find that out on the first call, which is why a good first call matters as much as the score.

faqs.q: Is a higher quality score always better?
faqs.a: Not always. A high score means the answers look favourable, but it says nothing about things the form does not ask, such as security or sector. Use it to rank leads you could place, not to replace your own judgement.

faqs.q: Why is a lead with a good score sometimes cheap?
faqs.a: Price depends on fundability, including affordability. If the amount asked for is far above what the business's revenue supports, the lead is priced low even if credit and trading time look fine.

faqs.q: Does the score change after I buy?
faqs.a: The score is based on the answers given on the form, so it describes the enquiry as submitted. What you learn on the first call is yours to record in your own notes and pipeline.

faqs.q: Can I filter by quality score?
faqs.a: You can filter the Opportunities list and set auto-buy criteria around the underlying answers, such as credit history, revenue and time trading. These shape the quality of what you see and buy.

faqs.q: Is the score a credit score?
faqs.a: No. It is not a credit reference score. It combines the credit history answer with time trading, revenue, urgency and existing debt, all taken from the enquiry form.
